text: 3. Methodology

In this section, we first formulate the CTR prediction problem and then introduce our proposed framework, CETNet , as shown in Figure 1 . Although our experiments focus on ensembling two of Meta’s models, InterFormer and DHEN, the framework is general and can extend to ensemble [MATH N] N N models. The key components include multi-embedding paradigm 3.2 , a collaborative learning mechanism 3.3 , and a softmax-based confidence fusion module 3.4 .
3.1. Problem Formulation

The goal of CTR prediction task is to estimate the probability that a user will click on a given item. Formally, let [MATH \mathcal{U}] 𝒰 \mathcal{U} denote the set of users and [MATH \mathcal{I}] ℐ \mathcal{I} denote the set of items. For each user [MATH u\in\mathcal{U}] u ∈ 𝒰 u\in\mathcal{U} and item [MATH i\in\mathcal{I}] i ∈ ℐ i\in\mathcal{I} , the objective is to learn a function [MATH \hat{\text{y}}=f(u,i,x)] y ^ = f ⁡ ( u , i , x ) \hat{\text{y}}=f(u,i,x) that predicts [MATH \hat{\text{y}}] y ^ \hat{\text{y}} , the probability of a click, where [MATH x] x x represents the associated features. The input features [MATH x] x x consist of three types: sparse features [MATH x_{\text{sparse}}] x sparse x_{\text{sparse}} , dense features [MATH x_{\text{dense}}] x dense x_{\text{dense}} , and sequence features [MATH x_{\text{seq}}^{u}] x seq u x_{\text{seq}}^{u} . Sparse features are categorical data such as user ID, item ID, and item category, which are mapped to dense vectors via embedding tables, represented as [MATH x_{\text{sparse}}=\{x_{\text{id}}^{u},x_{\text{id}}^{i},x_{\text{cat}}^{i},\dots\}] x sparse = { x id u , x id i , x cat i , … } x_{\text{sparse}}=\{x_{\text{id}}^{u},x_{\text{id}}^{i},x_{\text{cat}}^{i},\dots\} . Dense features are continuous values, such as a user’s age or an item’s price, used either directly or after normalization, represented as [MATH x_{\text{dense}}=\{x_{\text{age}}^{u},x_{\text{price}}^{i},\dots\}] x dense = { x age u , x price i , … } x_{\text{dense}}=\{x_{\text{age}}^{u},x_{\text{price}}^{i},\dots\} . Sequence features capture users’ historical interactions with items, represented as [MATH S^{u}=\{s_{1}^{u},s_{2}^{u},\dots,s_{N}^{u}\}] S u = { s 1 u , s 2 u , … , s N u } S^{u}=\{s_{1}^{u},s_{2}^{u},\dots,s_{N}^{u}\} , where [MATH u] u u denotes the specific user. The sequence is truncated or padded to a fixed length [MATH N] N N to ensure consistent input size, keeping only the most recent interactions if necessary or adding padding if the sequence is shorter. In real-world scenarios, users often generate multiple interaction sequences. We denote these sequences for a given user [MATH u] u u as [MATH S^{u}_{1},\dots,S^{u}_{k}] S 1 u , … , S k u S^{u}_{1},\dots,S^{u}_{k} , where [MATH k] k k is the total number of sequences associated with the user. Binary cross-entropy loss is the objective function for optimization.
3.2. Multi-Embedding Paradigm

Traditional CTR models typically use a single embedding table to transform categorical features into dense vector representations. However, relying on a single embedding table may limit the ability to capture the complex and diverse feature interaction patterns present in heterogeneous data. To address these limitations, previous work ( Guo et al., 2024 ) proposed the multi-embedding paradigm, which mitigates embedding collapse and improves scalability by leveraging multiple embeddings for enhanced feature interaction learning. Inspired by this paradigm, our framework employs two specialized models: DHEN and InterFormer, each equipped with its own embedding table. These models capture complementary feature interactions and ensure that the overall model benefits from diverse interaction patterns:

• DHEN ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) (Deep Hierarchical Ensemble Network) leverages multiple heterogeneous interaction modules to learn a hierarchy of interactions across different orders. Its hierarchical structure ensures that both low-order and high-order interactions are effectively captured, resulting in a more expressive feature representation. • InterFormer ( Zeng et al., 2024 ) conducts deep interaction learning across heterogeneous features (including dense, sparse, and sequence features). It selects relevant information effectively without relying on aggressive aggregation, preserving the quality of critical feature interactions.

By assigning each model its own independent embedding table, the framework ensures that both hierarchical and deep feature interactions are captured, enriching the overall expressiveness of the learned feature representations. Each model maintains a distinct embedding table: DHEN employs [MATH \mathbf{E}_{\text{DHEN}}] 𝐄 DHEN \mathbf{E}_{\text{DHEN}} , while InterFormer utilizes [MATH \mathbf{E}_{\text{IF}}] 𝐄 IF \mathbf{E}_{\text{IF}} . The sparse feature embeddings are retrieved through embedding lookups as follows:

By maintaining separate embedding tables and MLPs for each model, InterFormer and DHEN capture distinct yet complementary feature interactions. InterFormer is designed to emphasize sequential learning, effectively modeling temporal dependencies and patterns in user behavior. On the other hand, DHEN focuses on capturing complex, high-order, and hierarchical feature interactions, making it well-suited for identifying intricate relationships among features. This complementary design ensures that both models contribute unique strengths, enhancing the overall performance of the ensemble.
3.3. Collaborative Learning
3.3.1. Challenge.

In traditional ensemble models, individual models may dominate the learning process, leading to imbalanced performance ( Webb et al., 2019 ) . To address this, we adopt a collaborative learning approach, where InterFormer and DHEN are trained in parallel, each focusing on different feature interaction patterns. InterFormer specializes in processing heterogeneous features such as dense, sparse, and sequential data, while DHEN captures high-order feature interactions through its hierarchical structure.

One challenge in collaborative learning is ensuring that both models contribute meaningfully to the final prediction. Without proper coordination, one model could dominate, leading to imbalanced learning. To address this, we adopt a symmetric KL divergence term that aligns the predicted distributions of both models, encouraging mutual refinement without sacrificing their individual strengths. The symmetric KL divergence for a dataset with [MATH N] N N samples is the sum of the KL divergence in both directions:

[MATH \mathcal{L}_{kl}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(i)}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}},\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}})+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(i)}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}},\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}),] ℒ k ​ l = 1 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 N ℒ KL ( i ) ​ ( y ^ IF , y ^ DHEN ) + 1 2 ​ ∑ i = 1 N ℒ KL ( i ) ​ ( y ^ DHEN , y ^ IF ) , \mathcal{L}_{kl}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(i)}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}},\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}})+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(i)}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}},\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}), where the individual KL divergences for a sample [MATH i] i i are given by:

[MATH \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(i)}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}},\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}})=\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}\log\frac{\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}}{\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}}+(1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)})\log\frac{1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}}{1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}},] ℒ KL ( i ) ​ ( y ^ IF , y ^ DHEN ) = y ^ IF ( i ) ​ log ⁡ y ^ IF ( i ) y ^ DHEN ( i ) + ( 1 − y ^ IF ( i ) ) ​ log ⁡ 1 − y ^ IF ( i ) 1 − y ^ DHEN ( i ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(i)}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}},\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}})=\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}\log\frac{\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}}{\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}}+(1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)})\log\frac{1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}}{1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}},

[MATH \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(i)}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}},\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}})=\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}\log\frac{\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}}{\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}}+(1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)})\log\frac{1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}}{1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}}.] ℒ KL ( i ) ​ ( y ^ DHEN , y ^ IF ) = y ^ DHEN ( i ) ​ log ⁡ y ^ DHEN ( i ) y ^ IF ( i ) + ( 1 − y ^ DHEN ( i ) ) ​ log ⁡ 1 − y ^ DHEN ( i ) 1 − y ^ IF ( i ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}^{(i)}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}},\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}})=\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}\log\frac{\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}}{\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}}+(1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)})\log\frac{1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}^{(i)}}{1-\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}^{(i)}}. This refinement term encourages consistency between the two models while allowing them to focus on different aspects of the feature interactions.
3.3.2. Collaboration vs. Diversity.

Our framework leverages both collaborative learning and diversity to enhance ensemble performance. While collaboration and diversity might seem contradictory, they are complementary in our approach. The collaborative learning component, implemented with symmetric KL divergence, ensures balanced contributions from each model, preventing any single model from becoming overly dominant.

Diversity, in this context, refers to the variation in feature representations produced by the different models in the ensemble. By using distinct embedding tables and targeting different interaction patterns, sequential for InterFormer and hierarchical for DHEN, each model captures unique aspects of the data, adding diverse perspectives to the final prediction. Together, these mechanisms enable our framework to achieve robust predictions by balancing aligned learning goals with diverse feature representations.
3.4. Confidence-Based Fusion

Once the two models—InterFormer and DHEN—generate their respective embeddings, we combine them using a confidence-based fusion mechanism inspired by ( Han et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ) . This mechanism ensures that each model’s contribution is proportional to its confidence in the prediction. We use the negation entropy of each model’s predicted probability distribution to measure its confidence. Lower entropy indicates higher certainty, and thus a larger contribution to the final embedding. The entropy for each model is computed as:

[MATH H(P)=-\hat{y}\text{log}\hat{y}-(1-\hat{y})\text{log}(1-\hat{y}),] H ⁡ ( P ) = − y ^ ​ log ​ y ^ − ( 1 − y ^ ) ​ log ​ ( 1 − y ^ ) , H(P)=-\hat{y}\text{log}\hat{y}-(1-\hat{y})\text{log}(1-\hat{y}), where [MATH \hat{y}] y ^ \hat{y} is the prediction. Let [MATH P_{\text{IF}}] P IF P_{\text{IF}} and [MATH P_{\text{DHEN}}] P DHEN P_{\text{DHEN}} be the predicted probability distributions from InterFormer and DHEN, respectively. The inverse entropy for each model, which serves as the confidence score, is given by:

[MATH C_{\text{IF}}=-H(P_{\text{IF}}),\quad C_{\text{DHEN}}=-H(P_{\text{DHEN}}).] C IF = − H ⁡ ( P IF ) , C DHEN = − H ⁡ ( P DHEN ) . C_{\text{IF}}=-H(P_{\text{IF}}),\quad C_{\text{DHEN}}=-H(P_{\text{DHEN}}).

To ensure that the confidence values do not interfere with the gradient flow during back-propagation, we detach the entropy values from the computation graph. This prevents the confidence scores from affecting the updates to each model’s individual projection layer (MLP) applied to its output embedding.
3.4.1. Softmax Weight Calculation and Embedding Fusion
We apply the softmax function to the inverse entropy values to generate the fusion weights for the embeddings:

[MATH w_{\text{IF}}=\frac{\exp(C_{\text{IF}})}{\exp(C_{\text{IF}})+\exp(C_{\text{DHEN}})},\quad w_{\text{DHEN}}=\frac{\exp(C_{\text{DHEN}})}{\exp(C_{\text{IF}})+\exp(C_{\text{DHEN}})}.] w IF = exp ⁡ ( C IF ) exp ⁡ ( C IF ) + exp ⁡ ( C DHEN ) , w DHEN = exp ⁡ ( C DHEN ) exp ⁡ ( C IF ) + exp ⁡ ( C DHEN ) . w_{\text{IF}}=\frac{\exp(C_{\text{IF}})}{\exp(C_{\text{IF}})+\exp(C_{\text{DHEN}})},\quad w_{\text{DHEN}}=\frac{\exp(C_{\text{DHEN}})}{\exp(C_{\text{IF}})+\exp(C_{\text{DHEN}})}.
Using these weights, the final fused embedding [MATH \mathbf{e}_{\text{fused}}] 𝐞 fused \mathbf{e}_{\text{fused}} is computed via weighted concatenation as:

[MATH \mathbf{e}_{\text{fused}}=[w_{\text{IF}}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\text{IF}}\|w_{\text{DHEN}}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\text{DHEN}}],] 𝐞 fused = [ w IF ⋅ 𝐞 IF ∥ w DHEN ⋅ 𝐞 DHEN ] , \mathbf{e}_{\text{fused}}=[w_{\text{IF}}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\text{IF}}\|w_{\text{DHEN}}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\text{DHEN}}], where [MATH \mathbf{e}_{\text{IF}}] 𝐞 IF \mathbf{e}_{\text{IF}} and [MATH \mathbf{e}_{\text{DHEN}}] 𝐞 DHEN \mathbf{e}_{\text{DHEN}} are the embeddings generated by InterFormer and DHEN, respectively.
3.4.2. Final Prediction
The fused embedding [MATH \mathbf{e}_{\text{fused}}] 𝐞 fused \mathbf{e}_{\text{fused}} is used to generate the final prediction through a readout function:

[MATH \hat{\text{y}}_{\text{fused}}=\sigma(\mathbf{W}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\text{fused}}+b),] y ^ fused = σ ⁡ ( 𝐖 ⋅ 𝐞 fused + b ) , \hat{\text{y}}_{\text{fused}}=\sigma(\mathbf{W}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\text{fused}}+b), where [MATH \sigma(\cdot)] σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid activation function, [MATH \mathbf{W}] 𝐖 \mathbf{W} is the weight matrix, and [MATH b] b b is the bias term. This final prediction, [MATH \hat{\text{y}}_{\text{fused}}] y ^ fused \hat{\text{y}}_{\text{fused}} , represents the likelihood of a click event.
3.4.3. Benefits of Confidence-Based Fusion

The confidence-based fusion mechanism ensures that the model with higher prediction certainty has a greater influence on the final output. This adaptive strategy enhances prediction robustness by dynamically leveraging each model’s strengths for individual instances. Additionally, detaching the entropy values stabilizes learning by preventing unintended gradient flow through the confidence scores.
3.4.4. Objective Function
Our framework optimizes three key binary cross-entropy losses: one for the output of the DHEN model, one for the InterFormer model, and one for the fused output. We define a unified loss function as:

[MATH \mathcal{L}(\hat{\text{y}}_{i})=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\text{y}_{i}\log(\hat{\text{y}}_{i})+(1-\text{y}_{i})\log(1-\hat{\text{y}}_{i})\right),] ℒ ( y ^ i ) = − 1 N ∑ i = 1 N ( y i log ( y ^ i ) + ( 1 − y i ) log ( 1 − y ^ i ) ) , \mathcal{L}(\hat{\text{y}}_{i})=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(\text{y}_{i}\log(\hat{\text{y}}_{i})+(1-\text{y}_{i})\log(1-\hat{\text{y}}_{i})\right), where [MATH \text{y}_{i}] y i \text{y}_{i} is the ground truth label, [MATH \hat{\text{y}}_{i}] y ^ i \hat{\text{y}}_{i} is the predicted probability for the [MATH i] i i -th sample, and [MATH N] N N is the total number of samples. The specific losses for each component are expressed as:

[MATH \mathcal{L}_{\text{DHEN}}=\mathcal{L}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\text{IF}}=\mathcal{L}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\text{fusion}}=\mathcal{L}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{fused}}),] ℒ DHEN = ℒ ⁡ ( y ^ DHEN ) , ℒ IF = ℒ ⁡ ( y ^ IF ) , ℒ fusion = ℒ ⁡ ( y ^ fused ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{DHEN}}=\mathcal{L}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{DHEN}}),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\text{IF}}=\mathcal{L}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{IF}}),\quad\mathcal{L}_{\text{fusion}}=\mathcal{L}(\hat{\text{y}}_{\text{fused}}), where [MATH \textbf{e}_{\text{DHEN}},\textbf{e}_{\text{IF}},] e DHEN , e IF , \textbf{e}_{\text{DHEN}},\textbf{e}_{\text{IF}}, and [MATH \textbf{e}_{\text{fused}}] e fused \textbf{e}_{\text{fused}} are the embeddings from the DHEN model, InterFormer model, and the fused output, respectively. The final objective function is defined as:

[MATH \mathcal{L}_{\text{final}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{fusion}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{DHEN}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{IF}}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{kl},] ℒ final = ℒ fusion + ℒ DHEN + ℒ IF + α ​ ℒ k ​ l , \mathcal{L}_{\text{final}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{fusion}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{DHEN}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{IF}}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{kl}, where [MATH \alpha] α \alpha is a hyperparameter controlling the impact of the KL divergence term. This objective function ensures that all three outputs—DHEN, InterFormer, and the fused model—are optimized simultaneously. The use of symmetric KL divergence aligns the individual models’ predictions, enhancing collaboration and improving overall performance.
